title: Quantum simulation of field-tunable spin spectroscopy of the quantum magnet Cs2CoCl4 on a trapped-ion quantum computer
authors: Elias Kokkas, Nora Bauer, Justin Provazza, Mark E. Nowakowski, Kathleen Hamilton, Gilles Buchs, Andrew Sornborger, Travis S. Humble, Ananth Kaushik, Martin Roetteler
abstract: The collective excitation spectra of quantum magnets provide a direct test of quantum computers as tools for studying strongly correlated matter. Hardware noise limits the circuit depths available for these calculations, leaving the question of how much magnetic information can survive circuit compression. Using IonQ's 36 qubit Forte Enterprise processor, we simulate the magnetic excitation spectra and spin dynamics of a 36 site Heisenberg XXZ chain describing the quantum magnet Cs2CoCl4 in a transverse field using quantum circuits containing just 420 two qubit gates. The workflow combines an ancilla free local kick protocol with classical tensor network compression, encoding both ground state preparation and time evolution. The reconstructed dynamical structure factors capture the evolution from a broad two spinon continuum toward a dispersive branch with magnon character near the expected critical field. We observe an interesting field driven sign reversal of the nearest neighbor spin correlations which shows a complementary signature of this magnetic evolution. Our error mitigation methods bring the reconstructed total spectra into close agreement with density matrix renormalization group calculations, with Pearson correlation and structural similarity above 0.9 and normalized mean squared error below 0.15. We also perform comparisons with experimental inelastic neutron scattering measurements to connect the recovered excitations to the material's magnetic response. Our results demonstrate that circuit compression and error mitigation allow noisy quantum processors to recover both collective excitations and local magnetic correlations providing a quantitative benchmark for quantum spectroscopy and a basis for extending these methods to more complex magnetic systems.
summary: This paper uses a trapped-ion quantum computer to simulate the magnetic excitation spectra of the quantum magnet Cs2CoCl4. By combining advanced quantum protocols with error mitigation, the authors successfully recovered the system's collective excitations and local correlations. The results validate the use of noisy quantum hardware for quantitative studies of strongly correlated matter, benchmarking against DMRG calculations.
main_problem: The study aims to test quantum computers' ability to simulate the collective excitation spectra and spin dynamics of strongly correlated quantum magnets, specifically addressing the impact of hardware noise on recoverable magnetic information.
main_result: The quantum simulation successfully reconstructed the evolution of the excitation spectrum, showing agreement with DMRG benchmarks and connecting results to inelastic neutron scattering measurements.
method: The authors employed a quantum simulation protocol combining an ancilla-free local kick protocol with classical tensor network compression on a trapped-ion quantum computer.
model_or_system: The system is the quantum magnet Cs2CoCl4, modeled by an effective spin 1/2 XXZ Heisenberg chain Hamiltonian, which is studied across varying transverse magnetic fields.
key_observables: Dynamical Spin Structure Factor (DSF), Retarded Green's Function (RGF), and local magnetic correlations (e.g., nearest neighbor spin correlations).
important_parameters: System size L=36 sites, varying transverse field $h_x/J$ (e.g., 0 to 1.604), and time evolution steps up to $Jt=12$.
main_assumptions: The use of error mitigation techniques and classical circuit compression are necessary to overcome hardware noise limitations.
figures_summary: Figures compare the reconstructed Dynamical Structure Factor (DOS) from quantum hardware simulations against theoretical benchmarks like DMRG-CV and DMRG+Trotter, showing quantitative agreement.
paper_structure: The paper details the quantum protocol for measuring the retarded spin response, compares the results across different magnetic field regimes (Luttinger liquid to gapped/polarized phases), and validates the results using multiple quantitative metrics against established numerical methods.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, quantitative benchmark demonstrating how near-term quantum processors can tackle complex, strongly correlated many-body physics problems relevant to condensed matter theory.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Workflow for calculating the magnetic response. Top: the model of Cs2CoCl4 is a spin 1/2 XXZ chain with J = 0.23 meV, ∆= 0.25, and L = 36 sites. Classical DMRG and second order Trotter evolution supply reference states, which are approximated by circuits composed of D staircase layers of nearest neighbor two qubit blocks. The compressed circuits are executed on IonQ Forte Enterprise, and the measurements are used to reconstruct the retarded Green’s function, DSF, and local autocorrelations. FIG. 2. Fidelity of the compressed state preparations rela- tive to their classical targets. At tk = 0, the plotted quan- tity is the ground state fidelity F0 in Eq. (6). At nonzero times tk = k∆t, with ∆t = 0.6/J, the curves show the fidelity Fk in Eq. (15), averaged with equal weights over the three spin channels (xx, yy, zz). The ground state cir- cuits use (252, 315, 232, 77) two qubit gates at hx/J = (0, 0.764, 1.146, 1.604), respectively. Every nonzero time point uses 420 two qubit gates. These fidelities quantify how closely the compressed circuits approximate their classical tar- get states before hardware execution.
